responses.final.architecture_evidence: My node is reactive because the decide_velocity function only looks at the reading from front_distance and has no memory of previous scans or any of the internal states that describes what the robot is trying to do. Each decision is computed fresh from the latest sensor data alone. To make this a hybrid system it would need a deliberative layer on top. For example, a planner that maintains a map or goal, tracks the robot's position over time, and issues higher-level intentions, like navigating around an obstacle and reaching a specific point, that the reactive layer can then execute moment-to-moment for immediate safety.

responses.final.system_synthesis:
The robotics software that is used is difficult because it has to coordinate a lot at once. It makes sure that the physical hardware, real sensor noise, and timing constraints all work together simultaneously, while remaining safe because one bug or delay in the robot can produce a unsafe physical action, as opposed to an error message on a screen. The software we are used to have a less dangerous output, where a robot's output is a motion in the real world, making it harder to have a successful and safe outcome. In mission 3, I implemented a reactive architecture, where the robot's behavior is a direct function of its most recent sensor reading, with no internal model of past states or planned future actions. The function front_distance narrows down a full LiDAR sweep to the single closest obstacle ahead and decide_velocity converts that distance into a move or a stop. The trade-off here is that reactive systems are simple, fast, and easy to test when isolated, but the downside is that they can't plan ahead, remember context, or make more complex decisions like going around an obstacle. 

ROS 2 connected to many components through several communication relationships. The LiDAR driver publishes raw scan data on /scan. The obstacle_guard node subscribes to /scan, calls decision functions, and publishes a velocity command to ...cmd_vel. A supplied command guard node subscribes to cmd_vel and enforces safety limits before anything can even reach the robot. Lastly, the simulated robot subscribes to the guard's output to actually move. The relationship demonstrated here is a publish-subscribe one, chained together into a pipeline. 

Timing and invalid data both directly affected safety in this project. While I was debugging a rest command, I saw firsthand how a tight timeout time combined with normal ROS 2 discovery delay could cause a correct command to fail unexpectedly, which showed me why it is important to have a wider margin in timing and not just enough for the typical case duration, because more often than not it will never be the standard/expected time. Similarly, front_distance treats nan, inf, and any non-positive readings as invalid rather than assuming that they mean it is clear. This increases safety because we can't assume from missing data that something is clear when there is no real and verifiable information. 

The layer that could restrict unsafe motion is the command guard layer and this is because it independently checks the messages being received and acts as a final safety net.
responses.final.timing_evidence: Watching a correct and tested command intermittently fail because of a fixed timeout racing against normal ROS 2 discovery delay stood out the most. From this I was able to see that "correct logic" isn't sufficient on its own, a safety relevant action can fail but not because the code is wrong, but because the surrounding timing assumptions don't leave enough margin for the real-world variability.

responses.mission_3.data_to_command: front_distance() gets a bunch of readings that cover multiple directions but then narrows them down to ones that are in the front and have valid values, then picks the closest one. Decide_velocity uses that closest number and applies rules to it so it knows when to stop or continue moving.
responses.mission_3.missing_data_safety: This is because it is the safest and most reasonable option. No valid front measurement doesn't mean all clear so if we assume the path is clear that could be problematic because there is a high chance it is not clear. We can't treat the unknown like all clear because that is not the most careful option.
responses.mission_3.system_layers: The decision functions, the ROS node and command guard form a layered pipeline, where each piece is responsible for different parts of safety logic. The ROS node handles the ROS-specific tasks, like subscribing to /scan. It recieves raw LiDAR data and then publishes the result to ..cmd_vel. Every new scan the node with call the 2 functions in their respective sequence. frontD_distance() reduces the LiDAR ranges down to the closest valid obstacle that is directly ahead. Then that number gets converted into a forward speed with limits. The functions don't know anything about the ROS itself, they are just funtions who take in values and returns one singular value. The command guard is the safety check for messages that get published to cmd_vel. It can override or stop the robot if something is not right.
